As this trend continued through the 1950 Census, Census respondents were specifically asked to list their race, and the number of Hispanic respondents included in this count actually increased.

At the begin of the Holocene (~11,700 years ago), the Rhine occupied its Late-Glacial valley. As a meandering river, it reworked its ice-age braidplain. The ice-age glaciers that now dominate many Alpine lakes had retreated across northern Germany [1] and France [2]. As the glacier was advancing south, a series of tributaries from France began to cut through the Rhine and create a massive river delta in the North Sea. The final stages of the last glacier advance are usually thought of as being a series of events leading to the final retreat of the ice sheet at the end of the last glacial maximum about 23,300 years ago. However, a study suggested that the final phase of this final stage of glacier advance was not fully completed until 8600 years ago [3, 4].

It is assumed the last glacier advance over northern Germany was a global process of glacier recession. While this is the current consensus on glacier advance, it is now apparent that we have to consider the impact of regional and local processes on glacier advance. In particular, the glacier advance is constrained by the supply of meltwater to the ice sheet during the last major phase of glacier advance (11,700 years ago). There was probably not enough melt-water available for this entire glacier advance to finish before 8600 years ago [3]. Consequently, the glacier continued to advance south [4].

The glacier advance was a regional phenomenon spanning North Germany as far south as Switzerland and parts of the France Alps (Figure 1). A detailed reconstruction of the final glacier advance shows a total of eight significant phases of the advance [5, 6]. Of these, the last is believed to have occurred during the year 8600 years ago

At present, the Purus Arch is represented by the Rio Tocantins-Urupá River and, downstream, by the Tocantins River. The Purus Arch has produced two large tectonic events. The first was caused by an increase in lithospheric uplift associated with isostatic rebound after the uplift of the Andean chain (see section on the Andean Craton) at the end of the Oligocene and the second was caused by a decrease in lithospheric uplift after the uplift of the Amazonian plateau at the beginning of the Miocene. The tectonic split resulted in several large basins being separated. In the Purus Arch, the two largest are: the Tocantins River (Urupá Basin) and the Amazon River (Purus River Basin and Amazon Basin). The Tocantins River is nearly 2 km wide with a floodplain on the left bank and a delta on the right bank. The Amazon River is 7 km wide with a floodplain on the left bank and a delta on the right bank. The Amazon River also has an irregular floodplain, as the river is channeling through the Amazon basin, and there are three major channels in the Amazonian delta. The Amazon River Basin is drained by the Amazon-Urupá and Chico Mendes rivers.

Reciprocating piston type steam engines remained the dominant source of power until the early 20th century, when advances in the design of electric motors and internal combustion engines gradually resulted in the replacement of reciprocating (piston) steam engines in commercial usage, and the ascendancy of steam turbines in power generation. The most common reciprocating steam machine is now the water-tube engine, in which the working cylinder and piston reciprocate. Water-tube engines have a much higher torque to weight ratio than reciprocating steam engines, and they have a smaller cylinder, piston and valve space. Water-tube engines have had many practical applications in transportation and heavy equipment, though they are almost always used to drive reciprocating crankshafts or waterwheels. The steam turbine has been widely used for large generators for electric power distribution, as well as large motor and generators for large water-supply systems. There are currently over 15,000 water-tube engines, nearly all of which use a four-stroke work cycle operating in the so-called Rankine cycle.

Killer T cells are a sub-group of T cells that kill cells that are infected with viruses (and other pathogens), or are otherwise damaged or dysfunctional. As with B cells, each type of T cell recognizes a different antigen. Killer T cells are activated when their T cell receptor (TCR) binds to this specific antigen in a complex with the MHC Class I receptor of another cell. Killer T cells then undergo a rapid clonal expansion upon this stimulation. While it is thought that some killer T cells are activated from within the thymus (the site of MHC Class I receptor diversity acquisition), it is also possible that they are created by stimulation with MHC-molecules cross-reactive to viral protein.
Vβ Receptors on T cells have been extensively studied. They are used as molecules on T cell receptors that, upon cell binding, determine the specificity of the cells involved in killing. It has been shown that Vβ Receptors on T cells are used both by T cells to regulate their proliferation during development, and by T cells to generate killing capacity. Different T cell subpopulations may therefore use different Vβ Receptors to regulate their proliferation, while others may use different killer function. The identification of Vβ receptors involved in both regulation of proliferation and in the killing of cells infected with an antigen specific for them may therefore be useful for the development of new therapies aimed at treating disease.

From the Eocene onwards, the ongoing Alpine orogeny caused a N–S rift system to develop in this zone. The main elements of this rift are the Upper Rhine Graben, in southwest Germany and eastern France and the Lower Rhine Embayment, in northwest Germany and the southeastern Netherlands. By the time of the Miocene, a river system had developed in the Upper Rhine Graben, that continued northward and is considered the first Rhine river. A number of small basins were connected to the Rhine system, as the Rhos and the Ems basin in Belgium and the Halle basin in Switzerland. These formed the Lower German Rhine basin with two small parts along its borders. Later, a drainage system developed in central Europe to allow for the rise of high plateaus, the main mountain peaks of these basins. These peaks have a high relief, reaching to 3,700 m in the case of the Bernese Alps and 2,000 m in the case of the Jura mountains of France.

With the onset of the Neogene (Miocene), a long ice advance covered southern Europe from the north, a process which has continued to the present day. The advance resulted in a progressive uplift of the plateaus that separated the basins and resulted in new erosion areas. A series of erosive episodes occurred in the Rhine system, which resulted in the formation of numerous lakes and in the formation of basins like the Humber basin in the English Channel. These formed a major fault trace through the system. The N-border of the European ice sheet was shifted west at this time. However, both the Très ancien contoumier, from 1200 to 1245 and the Grand coutumier de Normandie were transcribed into the contemporary language of French for the general public, and are published by the French Government’s Departments.

The customs of the Normans are complex and multilayered. The customs of the region of Normandy are complex compared to many other regions in Europe; for example, the customs differ most drastically between Brittany and Normandy, between Normandy and the rest of France, and even between Brittany and England. Some of these customs persist to this very day, whereas others have been reduced to a few simple, and sometimes complex, laws. As we have seen in the previous chapter, many of the laws of Normandy remain largely the same to this day.

The customs of the Normans derive directly from their geography and were carried by the Normans along the route towards the European market from the 10th to the 13th centuries. Socialists attribute the vast disparities in wealth to the private ownership of the means of production by a class of owners, creating a situation where a small portion of the population lives off unearned property income by virtue of ownership titles in capital equipment, financial assets and corporate stock. By contrast, the vast majority of the population is dependent on income in the form of a wage or salary. In order to rectify this situation, socialists argue that the means of production should be socially owned so that income differentials would be reflective of individual contributions to the social product. This would eliminate income inequalities, because it would create a system where the owners are rewarded for labouring.

While the socialist vision of society has been gaining support, there are people, principally in the US, who continue to have issues with the idea of private ownership of the means of production. The reason socialism isn't adopted is because no one believes that it's fair that most of society be dependent on a small portion of society for its income. But then, at the so-called Rheinbrech, the Rhine water abruptly falls into the depths because of the greater density of cold water. The water slows to a crawl.

A fisherman in his kayak or canoe, wearing flippers so the fish won't snag in the legs and pull away, floats nearby. He is trying his best not to disturb the cold water. If the water suddenly disappears, he will yell and the boatman will come to get him.

The boatman arrives in a canoe or a little kayak, a huge aluminum tub that serves as both a hull and a boathouse. He begins to tow the kayak into the bow of the boat. The kayak, in his hands, slowly sinks until the water is so cold that he begins to be able to feel it, and the temperature of the water is no longer dropping. The sun is coming up. He holds the kayak as if it were a heavy object, like a log being slowly pushed or pulled into the water to keep itself from drifting away, for no reason. He pulls the kayak forward into the boat.

This kind of cold-water sport is called "kneadog" or "keadogting." Many kayakers are now using "kayak-kayak" instead of kayak, but that is the term used at the waterfowl and game warden headquarters.

Criminal punishment is typically applied when an offender is "guilty" according to the definition of their crime and there are no alternatives to conviction. In practice, however, it does not follow that the offender would have been convicted if an objective test could be devised to determine which crimes deserve to be punished for the purpose of incapacitation and/or deterrence (Witt 2013: 853f).

Consequently, criminal justice scholars such as Paul and DeJong (2000) reject the possibility that criminal punishment could be designed to control crime, because the main aim of criminal punishment is incapacitation. Likewise, John T. Reiner and his colleagues (2010) argue, at least in part, that deterrence and incapacitation are not, as is often claimed, inseparable concepts as one must incapacitate criminals to reduce crime (Reiner and Smith [2008]). These challenges, as well as the failure to repeat similar epidemics in areas of similar geography and socioeconomic status, have fuelled the argument that the Black Death was a'super-scorched-earth' plague that took many other forms and killed many less severely. However, these accounts must be considered in light of changing medical knowledge, which has highlighted the limitations of the infectious theory as a general explanation of the plague. However, even if new, better, evidence was to emerge regarding the plague's modes of transmission, the infectious nature of the virus itself might still give it a foothold as a cause of the Black Death.

Newly published genetic sequences (of samples from the Black Death in the Netherlands, dating from 1347 to 1352, and also three samples from the Spanish bubonic plague in the 16th century, one of which is also from the Black Death in Northern Africa) have been able to throw further light on the plague's origins with a single virus. John Dalton's original atomic hypothesis assumed that all elements were monatomic and that the atoms in compounds would normally have the simplest atomic ratios with respect to one another. In reality, atoms of different elements will often have different values for their atomic masses as well. But that makes it more difficult to understand the way these elements combine with other elements. Dalton used this complexity to argue that the elements do not come from one "big" nucleus but are composed of smaller ones. He proposed that an electric spark in a lightning bolt initiated this complicated process of atomic combination, making it all the way down from protons to electrons. But in the 1920s and '30s, it became clear that atoms exist that are not protons but other elements such as neutrons, lithium, carbon, oxygen and the rest of the elements. This meant that the elements have a complicated atomic structure.

Dalton never wrote an elaborate treatise on the atomic constitution of atoms. But his book 'A New System of the Chemical Nomenclature' did help to explain atomic and chemical structure

Of the 129 MSPs, 73 are elected to represent first past the post constituencies and are known as "Constituency MSPs". Voters choose one member to represent the constituency, and the member with most votes is returned as a constituency MSP. The 73 Scottish Parliament constituencies shared the same boundaries as the UK Parliament constituencies in Scotland, prior to the 2005 reduction in the number of Scottish MPs, with the exception of Orkney and Shetland which each return their own constituency MSP. The electorate can be increased in multi-member wards by voters who want to create wards more to their liking but does not elect a single MSP.

The Parliament of the United Kingdom has four 'Preside' constituencies, called Presiding Officers in Scotland. Both male and female Preside are allocated to Scotland, as is the case for members of the Scottish Parliament (they represent one part of Scotland, instead of being elected from all of Scotland). The Preside has no vote and does not vote. The Constitution of the Holyrood Parliament lists the current Presides: Scotland, Airdrie, Argyll and Bute, Falkirk, Linlithgow and East = Stirling and Glasgow South West. There are 17 MSPs from Scotland, with six from Airdrie, three from Argyll and Bute, three from Falkirk and four from Linlithgow and East = Stirling, Glasgow and South West, with the additional seat of East Lothian in the East Region. From the whole of England, only one MSP is elected to represent Scotland at Westminster: the Speaker.

The Scottish Parliament has been established for 25 years. It is the only devolved legislature in the United Kingdom, apart from the European Parliament for Scotland. There are now 93 MSPs (and two additional MP's) from Scotland, all of whom have been elected to represent constituencies.

In each case, we investigate the effect of capital accumulation and capital depreciation on the long-run rate of profit. Our main results are summarized as follows. First, capital accumulation by private firms reduces the long-run rate of profit. Second, the decline in the long-run rate of return due to capital accumulation can be either the result of the increase in capital depreciation or the result of the decrease in net national income.

1. Introduction3 The issue of capital accumulation under a system of national income accounting is of great interest to both scholars and policymakers. One reason is that the theory is well developed and well supported by a sizable body of empirical research conducted over the years. Yet, the discussion about the effect of capital accumulation on the long-term rate of profit is often at best superficially based. We address this gap in our second contribution, by offering a theoretical analysis that seeks to identify the key factors responsible for changes in the long-run rate of profit in both open economy models and closed economy models of corporate taxes. As our third contribution in this paper, we also examine the impact of capital depreciation on the long-run rate of return in both the open and closed economy models.

The innate response is usually triggered when microbes are identified by pattern recognition receptors, which recognize components that are conserved among broad groups of microorganisms, or when damaged, injured or stressed cells send out alarm signals, many of which (but not all) are recognized by the same receptors as those that recognize pathogens. Innate immune defenses are non-specific, meaning these systems respond to pathogens in a generic way. This means that despite the diversity of microorganisms that a host is exposed to, each interacts with the immune system in the same ways. The microbes that survive the immune response, and continue to replicate, are themselves a source of harm. In most cases, the surviving microbes continue to stimulate inflammation that can lead to the development of immune-mediated disease.

The purpose of the innate immune system of humans is to protect the body from injury and infection. The response consists of two phases: inflammation and repair. In the inflammation phase, proinflammatory signals are induced that act locally and result in the destruction of injurious cell populations, including those that cause immune-mediated diseases. In the repair phase, the proinflammatory signals are quickly resolved. Together, these reactions initiate the removal of the injurious cell populations and initiate repair of the injurious tissue.

Two key events control the inflammatory and repair phases. Two years later, the patient underwent an excisional biopsy for a suspected breast mass. Histopathological examination confirmed an invasive ductal carcinoma. The excised breast area was free of invasive diseases, but two small surgical scars had developed as a result of the previous surgery. Five years after excision of the two surgical scars, the patient noticed a breast mass by palpation. Histopathological examination revealed an invasive infiltrating ductal carcinoma. The two invasive primary lesions were removed by wide excision. In the specimen obtained from the excisional biopsy, there was no evidence of invasive cancer in the ipsilateral breast tissues but a small invasive tumour in the contralateral breast. Therefore, wide excision of large breast tissue was performed on both the tumour side and the healthy adjacent portion, including the scar. The pathological diagnosis was infiltrating ductal carcinoma of the contralateral breast, and the pathological stage was IA. The scars on the surgical site were managed conservatively, and were not excised. Five years after excision of the invasive tumour, the patient is well without recurrence. To the best of the authors' knowledge, there have been no other previous reports similar to this disease pattern arising in a surgical scar. According to the literature, the main problem of this disease is the difficulty in establishing the correct diagnosis and the need for a careful follow-up, particularly for a patient in whom surgical treatment could be contraindicated. The history of MPD/MSS is similar to that of the Internet, but it has undergone a far greater number of iterations and developments. In the early days, it was used as a means of transferring files, email, and other messaging protocols to large, unreliable, highly asymmetric networks. In this manner, each party that wishes to communicate directly with the other may transmit its message to the other party, who must then decrypt it in order to learn the message. The public-key system is more secure in that anyone who learns the private key can in theory send other messages to any party (even your partner) who could decrypt them, because the third party does not have the private key itself.

One of the more notable applications of printing technology was the chao, the paper money of the Yuan. Chao were made from the bark of mulberry trees. The Yuan government used woodblocks to print paper money, but switched to bronze plates in 1275. The printing office's job was to produce paper money. The chao were printed in batches with three or four plates to a roll for each batch. Each batch included twenty-four to thirty-two plates. The print job was assigned by lot. The printing shop had several hundred workers.

An inscription on the print plate was the first thing noticed. It was a formula made out of a variety of words, not from a recipe book. Some print plates had Chinese characters, some roman; there was some German. After that came the date and the year. There was the amount of ink needed, some Chinese symbols, and an "indentation line" for the amount left on the roll.

Stage 1 is the first, or introductory stage of the bill, where the minister or member in charge of the bill will formally introduce it to Parliament together with its accompanying documents – Explanatory Notes, a Policy Memorandum setting out the policy underlying the bill, and a Financial Memorandum setting out the costs and savings associated with it. This is followed by a second stage, Stage 2, where the bill can be debated on the floor of Parliament, to determine if it should enter into Committee stage.

A government bill will not enter into Committee stage (if it is proposed by a government) until it has been considered by at least two committees of which at least one has accepted it. If the bill is accepted by two or more committees (and accepted by at least two members in each committee – not by the relevant House or by a party caucus), the Minister will present it to the Cabinet for review on 4 May. If the Cabinet confirms acceptance, it becomes ‘scheduled’, but will not come into effect immediately. If the bill is not accepted by the Cabinet, it will come in for second stage consideration, on 5 May. This will be a final attempt to pass the bill on the floor of Parliament and if it does not pass, it will be returned to the first stage. While it is on second stage on 5 May, the bill remains on the agenda.

A government bill can be debated in two stages by different committees (sometimes the same committee), although it will always be debated on both stages (the first and second). Specialty pharmacies supply high cost injectable, oral, infused, or inhaled medications that are used for chronic and complex disease states such as cancer, hepatitis, and rheumatoid arthritis. Unlike a traditional community pharmacy where prescriptions for any common medication can be brought in and filled, specialty pharmacies carry novel medications that need to be properly stored, administered, carefully monitored, and clinically managed. In addition to supplying these drugs, specialty pharmacies also provide lab monitoring, adherence counseling, and assist patients with cost-containment strategies needed to obtain their expensive specialty drugs.

A growing public fear exists regarding the increasing cost of specialty drugs among Medicare beneficiaries. An increase in the cost of specialty drugs could mean a loss to the Medicare program and ultimately the beneficiary of any drug program. A recent analysis of the Medicare population shows that the cost of specialty medications is one of the largest component of total drug expenditures. Moreover, specialty drugs account for a full third of the drug expenditures and they are expected to rise as they become more costly for the Medicare program.

There are significant differences between the prescription drug market and the specialty pharmacy market. For instance, a drug's cost does not have to meet the regulatory benchmark for a drug, nor does the same drug have to be covered by Medicare Part D. In addition, the pharmaceutical benefit manager (PBMs) that pays for specialty drugs does not have to monitor specialty drugs as PBMs do with prescription drugs.

Medicare beneficiaries are unique in several ways that impact purchasing specialty drugs. Medicare patients are more comfortable with generic drugs. The public also has more trust in traditional pharmacies that provide "generic drugs" at the convenience of the pharmacy in contrast to the specialty pharmacy marketplace where drug manufacturers have their drugs distributed. Lastly, specialty pharmacies have different business models that may allow patients to receive higher brand-name drugs at lower drug co-pays. These differences increase the potential for drug cost savings when specialty pharmacies are used as a health plan drug store or managed care provider.

Thus we were treated to every scene between Elizabeth and Darcy taking place outside for no apparent reason, in inappropriately rugged scenery and often in the pouring rain. Not to mention that Jane Austen, and in particular P & P, is not about passion, sexual tension or love. It's about all those other things. And if you don't like the movie because it's not like the book, then you can be just as happy to enjoy the beautiful, carefully crafted world, the way it was originally meant to be seen. I'm not talking about a love-hate relationship from which we are left with the impression that something has been lost in the translation from Jane Austen's to this new version. (It's also possible the adaptation is too careful with that part of the film.) Oxygen is a chemical element with symbol O and atomic number 8. It is a member of the chalcogen group on the periodic table and is a highly reactive nonmetal and oxidizing agent that readily forms compounds (notably oxides) with most elements. By mass, oxygen is the third-most abundant element in the universe, after hydrogen and helium. It is the fourth-most abundant element in air and the fourth in water, after hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen. It is the most common by weight in the Earth's crust and ocean water; it is about 40 percent less common in the air, and it is only slightly more abundant in soils.

Oxygen is found in air, water, and other common organic compounds. Water, in particular, is made up essentially of oxygen and hydrogen; all of the other elements other than hydrogen are in the form of hydrogen molecules and the heavier elements in group 1 (or group 2) have their valence shells filled above the group 1 or 2 atom. The light elements in group 1 (oxygen, hydrogen, fluorine, magnesium) have a single valence shell (a closed group 2 atom) in which the valence electrons are completely removed; thus these have a net negative charge and are electroneutral. The valence electrons of the more common atoms in group 1 (helium, neon, sodium, &c.) are partially removed in the formation of electrons in the outer shells of the respective elements in their group. A couple of companies, Hartford Carpet and Bigelow Carpet, were so incensed they took the Dobsons all the way to the highest court in the land. The firms were quite right to be upset, the Supreme Court agreed, but then it got more complicated.

They had a few big things going for them, the justices reasoned: Hartford and Bigelow had worked together, and Dobson hadn't been directly selling anything. But the real question was whether those design ideas had ever been in the open long enough to be considered for copyright on the first of August 1885—which was when, according to the text of the judgment, you have to make copies of copyrighted designs or risk having them destroyed.

As for the Dobsons, they had been making copies. And using them. But they hadn't given a copyright notice beforehand. And Hartford and Bigelow hadn't made the same mistake. So this was not a case of the government seizing copyrighted works without notice, but of Dobson copyrighting a design without copyright notice.

Hyperbaric (high-pressure) medicine uses special oxygen chambers to increase the partial pressure of O 2 around the patient and, when needed, the medical staff. Carbon monoxide poisoning, gas gangrene, and decompression sickness (the 'bends') are sometimes treated using these devices. Increased O 2 concentration in the lungs helps to displace carbon monoxide from the heme group of hemoglobin. Carbon monoxide binds to and saturates hemoglobin where it can then no longer act as a source of O 2.

Inhalation anesthetics

We generally don't breathe pure oxygen in the air but instead use nitrous oxide and oxygen, also referred to as 'inhalation anesthetics'. Nitrous oxide is a colorless, odorless gas with a sweet, sweet smell. Nitrous oxide comes in a variety of concentrations, and comes in 100% N2O (pure nitrous oxide), 75% NO2 (pure nitrous oxide), 50% N2O2, and a mixture of 85% NO2 and 15% N2O.

Nitrous oxide has a low flash point of 32° centigrade making it difficult to sterilize with a hot water steam sterilizer. It has been in use since the 1930s for treating a variety of medical conditions,

An oscillating cylinder steam engine is a variant of the simple expansion steam engine which does not require valves to direct steam into and out of the cylinder. Instead of valves, the entire cylinder rocks, or oscillates, such that one or more holes in the cylinder line up with holes in a fixed port face or in the pivot mounting (trunnion). These engines are mainly used in toys and models, because of their simplicity, but have also been used in full size working engines, mainly on ships where their compactness is valued. They can also be used on small boats. Other uses are for toy model locomotives and trains, in which case these engines would not be oscillating at all, but would rock in a linear direction of the wheels, with many different engines rocking in this manner have been designed, sometimes with the aim of having a completely symmetrical locomotive in the field of locomotion.

The term "rotating cylinder" appears to be a misnomer. A true rotating cylinder would be difficult to make with only rotors, because the design would have to keep the piston moving within the cylinder throughout the rotation, which would mean that the cylinder would have to be made much longer than the crank shaft to fit inside.

The concept of legal certainty is recognised one of the general principles of European Union law by the European Court of Justice since the 1960s. Legal certainty is a notion which means the impossibility of proving a given legal position, or at least of finding another legal position under which a given legal position would have been proved if the legal position had been in doubt. The scope and meaning of this concept has changed very considerably over the last 40 years.

In the beginning, legal certainty was seen in terms of the law of the land. According to the concept, a national law is to be seen as the equivalent of the law of all citizens of a state. Accordingly, as a general rule of international law, a state has the power to decide any matter (other than to enter into a binding international legal agreement) upon the basis of the law of its own territory alone. Since it seems more sensible to deal with the law on a national level rather than to treat all law as being derived from the law of the land, the rule is often presented as “when in doubt, take the law of the state down to the letter”.

In the second half of the 20th century, the concept expanded further. It was extended further to include also international agreements of equal, though not all-embracing, scope—in other words, treaties which by their nature were not national treaties.

The principle of cross-cutting relationships pertains to the formation of faults and the age of the sequences through which they cut. Faults are younger than the rocks they cut; accordingly, if a fault is found that penetrates some formations but not those on top of it, then the formations that were cut are older than the fault, and the ones that are not cut must be younger than the fault. On the other hand, a fault may cut more than a single formation, but no more than one at a time. A cross-cutting relationship does not mean an exact relationship among the formations, and may be much different from the one one perceives when the fault in question is approached as a cross-cutting path. A relationship may be much more like that which one would expect if faulting occurred at great distances and under different fault planes. The question of whether P equals NP is one of the most important open questions in theoretical computer science because of the wide implications of a solution. If the answer is yes, many important problems can be shown to have more efficient solutions. These include various types of integer programming problems in operations research, many problems in logistics, protein structure prediction in biology, and the ability to find formal proofs of pure mathematics theorems. The most popular approach would be to show that P = NP. However, this is a very difficult task since no such proof has been found yet. A few of the most powerful techniques used against finding a proof are "bait and switch" techniques.

Bait Theories

Bait theories try to make it as difficult as possible for a human computer to solve the problem. For instance, if a human only wants to solve a problem in, say, two days, they may try a very difficult problem first. If they fail to solve it, they may then try easier problems. Bait theory works the same way. Bait is a mathematical problem that looks like the real thing, but the problem is much easier to solve. The advantage of a good bait theory over a good bait is that it makes finding the real thing very difficult.

Another way to explain bait theory is to consider a very simple human versus machine comparison: How difficult would it be for a human to find the root of a tree? Most or all of the tree will be below the root, so no search is needed. Suppose, however, you had a computer and asked it what the root had to do to find it. It may start searching from one of its own nodes instead of the root. This way it will get off far faster. The problem is one of time. Bait theory would be used as a bait to create an algorithm that would fail to find the root because it was too complex. An example of a simple bait for a tree problem would be to show the tree as a graph, but let the root node be a loop

One of the most prominent Huguenot refugees in the Netherlands was Pierre Bayle. Bayle is mostly known for his 17th century support for the Catholic Church and his attacks on the Protestant clergy and his own religious views. He is considered a controversial figure who was sometimes accused of being an atheist and was an avid supporter of the English political views of William of Orange at the same time, and later when the Dutch Republic was established in 1649. 

Pierre Bayle also took issue with the new, secular state of France and made several well-publicized criticisms against the church and the Catholic Church. While he had the last word in these conflicts, he was never publicly a supporter of Napoleon's campaign against the clergy. This is why he is often wrongly accused of being an atheist, and why he is still known as an anti-clerical figure in French history. In fact, he did often challenge the hierarchy and state in the interest of freedom and the Catholic faith in France.

However, Pierre Bayle was in fact one of the most prominent advocates of reason in France. After having initially supported the Royalist party against the monarchy, he eventually ended the anti-revolutionary faction, and instead was able to bring about a republic in 1792. However, this didn’t stop him maintaining a strong independence from the state, and his writings have continued to speak out against religion and government.

The Cestida ("belt animals") are ribbon-shaped planktonic animals, with the mouth and aboral organ aligned in the middle of opposite edges of the ribbon. There is a pair of comb-rows along each aboral edge, and tentilla emerging from a groove all along the oral edge, which stream back across most of the wing-like body surface. Cestids can swim by undulating their bodies as well as by the beating of their comb-rows.

Cestoids are euryhaline (nektonic) predators, feeding mostly on diatoms, with an occasional predation of other small zooplankton. Cestoids have well-developed eyes and vision, and are most active during night, but are visually guided mainly to prey (often in a haphazard pattern) and to nearby conspecifics. Feeding can proceed by the predator turning its head or by its movements, so it is a passive visual feeder; predators of cestoids will generally be able to follow their prey with their own eyes.

The simplest valve gears give events of fixed length during the engine cycle and often make the engine rotate in only one direction. Most however have a reversing mechanism which additionally can provide means for saving steam as speed and momentum are gained by gradually "shortening the cutoff" or rather, shortening the admission event; this in turn proportionately lengthens the expansion period. Where a non-reversing but open-center construction is employed, a steam "shortcut" is effected in the reverse direction without changing the length of the expansion.

For those cases where a fully "open-center" arrangement will rotate the engine in more than one direction for the use and efficiency of the steam as a motive power to the engine, one must provide a "variable-length" valve gear by controlling opening of the intake in one direction at an angle to the intake and with varying length to the point where the intake is stopped and opened in the opposite direction at an angle to the intake. The engine also can be arranged so that the steam flows in another direction and through different porting and at an angle to the intake. Such variable-length, or variable-width, arrangements will be useful for controlling steam pressure. Since its founding, the EU has operated among an increasing plurality of national and globalising legal systems. This has meant both the European Court of Justice and the highest national courts have had to develop principles to resolve conflicts of laws between different systems. Within the EU itself, the Court of Justice's view is that if EU law conflicts with a provision of national law, then EU law has primacy. In practice there are, nonetheless, numerous areas where one country's law prevails (i.e. the United Kingdom over Ireland, the United States over the Commonwealth and so on). A further complication arises when the EU has no authority over domestic law.

The European Parliament must be able to legislate, for example, on health and environmental matters. The European Commission must have legal competence to interpret EU rules and ensure their proper implementation. There are, nevertheless, various issues where the European Union lacks legal competence, e.g. on how to prevent people entering the Union from non-jurisdictional EU countries whose laws are unenforceable in the EU. Such "ex post" decisions by the European Court have given rise to arguments over whether EU law has, at all, primacy.

A key legal point to clarify is this: under certain conditions, the European Union has primacy and jurisdiction over the majority of member states. It is within these conditions that a court has primacy and jurisdiction over domestic law in a particular case. Some nations within the EU may have such a legal framework of their own that the primacy of their laws in such cases would be a matter of dispute, particularly in the field of consumer protection.

James Hutton is often viewed as the first modern geologist. In 1785 he presented a paper entitled Theory of the Earth to the Royal Society of Edinburgh. In his paper, he explained his theory that the Earth must be much older than had previously been supposed in order to allow enough time for mountains to be eroded and for sediments to form new rocks at the bottom of the sea, which in turn were raised up to become dry land. In addition to the study of rocks, Hutton also studied the geological processes that allowed Earth to become the planet we are on. While looking for suitable meteorites to study in this quest, Hutton discovered some of the planet’s meteoroids (comet fragments). A meteor is a small piece of something that impacts the Earth when out in the solar system. Meteoroids are small pieces of a more massive body, such as a planet’s or moon’s surface or debris from the parent body that broke away.

Hutton’s theory about how the Earth’s formation began has a name: geologic time. Hutton claimed that rocks had been in existence at the Earth’s surface for approximately twice the amount of time it took for the planet to form. According to this, rocks had been in existence as the Earth cooled and was able to form and erode in roughly the current age. The property of being prime (or not) is called primality. A simple but slow method of verifying the primality of a given number n is known as trial division. It consists of testing whether n is a multiple of any integer between 2 and . In other words, it consists of testing whether n divides x. For example, if n=53 and x is the integer 2, this procedure will yield true if and only if x is a multiple of 2; if it is not, then every prime number larger than 53 will prove to be an integer and hence n, after all, is not prime. Hence there are prime numbers larger than 53, which may prove that some integer is not a multiple of itself, a classic test for being not prime.

In general, if k is a prime number, then x is a multiple of k.

A prime number k is called the fundamental prime (or prime of the first kind, i.e., the only one among the first k primes) of a number n. It is said to be the smallest and the largest fundamental primes of n. (See below for examples.)

A lot of today's movies show war as an opportunity to highlight the ""hero's"" and other glamorous features of war, but very little attempts to show the true effect war actually takes on a community. The movie does a decent job of painting that it is indeed a loss and not an opportunity for those who do not have to bear the burden of war. That it takes a great deal of endurance and strength to carry out that burden as well. It's a powerful reminder about the human toll war takes on those who willingly take to it, and how much courage and support this one family has shown one another during the worst times of war.

we assume that , in equilibrium , nuclear matter at reduced density and moderate finite temperature , breaks up into many fragments . In the case of the breakup of a stable nuclei into many atomic nuclei, the fragments then become free and the thermal motion of the fragments becomes important. The internal structures of the fragments determine their properties; for instance, for the breakup of a spherical nucleus by many fission fragments, the fragments behave at their internal temperatures with an expansion at short distances and a compression at long distances, which is the same expansion and compression as that observed for the nuclear fission of a spherical system. This behaviour is known as shell effect [@Fro] or Jost effect [@Jost; @Rac]. However, for a nucleus undergoing fragmentation, the internal structures of the fragments are determined by their total masses. The fragmentation is then determined entirely by their masses, and the expansion for the fragments can no longer be assumed as that of a non-interacting many-body system. Hence, an analytic treatment without a free parameter is not feasible.

In this work we present results of a simulation of the disintegration of a spherical nucleus due to the fragmentation of the nucleus in the form of many fission fragments. It is tempting to think that the notion of function problems is much richer than the notion of decision problems. However, this is not really the case, since function problems can be recast as decision problems.

One of our goals in this section is to illustrate the difference between the two categories.

There is a great difference between deciding a given function and deciding whether the given function is continuous on a given interval. The first decision problem asks whether the given function is continuous for a given input range, but the second question requires looking to the function values or partial derivatives at the given input.

Given an input range, a function is continuous if all the partial derivatives are equal to zero for that range. That is to say, the function is continuous if its partial derivatives are equal to zero at any point.

That decision problem is easy for a computer: We can check it by simulating the function on a machine and seeing if a value is accepted on this machine. The only hard part is checking whether the partial derivatives are all equal and equal to zero.

text: 28 May 2016Until recently, the concept of generators, or resumable functions, seemed to me like a cute idea with only niche use cases. Sure, I had heard that generators in python and javascript could make certain things much nicer, but how often does one really need to have what appears to be nothing more than a fancy iterator? It wasn't until I followed this Rust RFC thread that the true potential of generators in Rust started to dawn on me. My first reaction to his proposal is "well, this doesn't look great!" Sure, the idea of generators in programming languages sounds magical; it should probably be a requirement for all of our programming languages at this point. But once I dug into the proposal, I realized that this is a good thing; there is an abundance of good things about generators in programming languages. The Lobata have a pair of lobes, which are muscular, cuplike extensions of the body that project beyond the mouth. Their inconspicuous tentacles originate from the corners of the mouth, running in convoluted grooves and spreading out over the inner surface of the lobes (rather than trailing far behind, as in the Cydippida). Between the lobes on either side of the mouth, many species of lobates have four auricles, gelatinous projections edged with cilia that produce water currents that help direct microscopic prey toward the mouth. (The four, like tentacles, are not really lobes, but lobate extensions of the mouth.) The mouth itself opens in about three minutes, and the tiny creatures swim in a single school at the center of the lobe. (The smaller lobates, or "fids," have no cilia, and swim alone, with their cilia facing the surface.) The two lobes are held together with strong suckers, which, like the stomachs of lobates and their closest relatives (which are all related to the Ediacarida), can hold water in an internal bag until used. In the morning, as the tide comes in, the two lobes turn against each other, squeezing water through these tubes and forcing all of the small prey into the mouth, where the fids will digest them. Most of the water they feed upon, however, remains in their stomachs. Only small lobates, including juvenile ones, make it to the surface of the ocean, where they swim long distances through the sea. The juveniles, which remain attached to the parents with powerful suckers, make it to the surface—but then they remain suspended for three or four days, and eventually starve.

For many Cnidaria, these microscopic feeding habits provide a means of finding food that is difficult or dangerous for larger animals. The young, for example, feed off their parents only for a couple of days, then are rescued by plankton that forms a large column near the oceanic surface, sometimes more than two hundred meters tall.

This change in the nature of an immune response has two implications. In the present case the Court of Justice considered it appropriate and necessary to achieve the same objective — public security of the UK and of the Member States. The court therefore had to decide whether the measures imposed (the expulsion procedures) were proportionate.

The Court of Justice found in favour of the UK. In the course of its opinion the court acknowledged:

That proportionality is necessary to ensure that the protection of citizens is taken seriously and not just limited to criminal offences.

That the objective of the UK and of the Member States, as regards the protection of society and public security, was the same:

That proportionality is not defined in EU law in a neutral or abstract manner. Rather, it is a legal principle that must be applied where the law being applied is not based on a clear distinction between public interest and private interests.

That proportionality should be read with regard to the circumstances and the specific context of the case and is a particular and sometimes specific issue.

According to this particular law principle proportionality concerns whether the means used have been the most appropriate and the most useful. The usual findings in these cases are severe eosinophilia, and hyperferritinemia with a concomitant rise in the transferrin saturation, i.e. the saturation of the transferrin- iron complex. the patient develops severe anemia and neutropenia due to iron-deficiency with a reduced availability of heme. Cgd with hyperferritinemia usually presents in the second decade and is associated with a mild to moderate thrombotic tendency, which is frequently complicated by thrombotic microangiopathies. it appears to be less prevalent than thrombotic-procoagulant syndromes. We report two cases of a cgd diagnosed in a patient with no symptoms in the absence of a co-existent thrombotic condition.

Methods - In this single-institution retrospective review of patients referred from colorectal surgery centers in the UK, we evaluated outcomes and the creation of a permanent stoma in patients treated with neoadjuvant chemoradiation for locally advanced rectal cancer.

Results - Patients with a permanent stoma after neoadjuvant chemoradiation were more likely to have undergone lymph node dissection and to have residual disease (50-60% of cases) and this relationship was independent of chemoradiation type (for stage II, a significant relationship was found between the need for and duration of permanent stoma and radiation dose, and for stage IIIA, there was a significant relationship between the need for and duration of permanent stoma and the use of adjuvant chemotherapy). The use of neoadjuvant chemotherapy was independently associated with a higher risk of permanent stoma.

Conclusions - Neoadjuvant chemoradiation is an effective option for the treatment of patients with locally advanced rectal cancer who are fit to receive surgery, and is associated with a low risk of permanent stoma. There is an association between a permanent stoma and the use of adjuvant chemotherapy, but this does not appear to be a reliable marker of poor oncological outcome.

Oxygen presents two spectrophotometric absorption bands peaking at the wavelengths 687 and 760 nm. Some remote sensing scientists have proposed using the measurement of the radiance coming from vegetation canopies in those bands to characterize plant health status from a satellite platform. This approach exploits the fact that in those bands it is possible to discriminate the vegetation's reflectance from its fluorescence, which is much weaker. The method was first studied by Förster and Zweifel in the infrared region and was further extended to the visible region by several researchers [7–9]. To date, however, this method has not been used for the remote sensing of the chlorophyll fluorescence in the spectral region of interest in this paper. Instead, the technique has focused mainly on the spectral region of the water absorption bands (2500–2500 nm) [6] or on the visible and near-infrared regions [3, 10].

An alternative approach is based on measuring the redder band centered around 615 nm, which corresponds to the emission of chlorophyll present in plant leaves [8, 11–13]. This red band is a clear sign of chlorophyll that is in decay [15, 16]. The magnitude of this band is influenced by both the chlorophyll content and the type of plant tissue – leaves being richer in chlorophyll than stems. In addition, the intensity of the red band declines more rapidly with increasing leaf age for photosynthetically active leaves with higher chlorophyll content [17, 18].

Although it is generally acknowledged that the red band is particularly sensitive to the health condition of the plant, in fact it is poorly understood why the red band is better for detecting chlorophyll changes in mature plants. results for monte carlo calculations of the electromagnetic vector and scalar form factors of the pion in a quenched simulation are presented . In quenched simulations, only valence quarks participate in the nucleon. It is therefore not expected to exhibit similar features to those encountered in the simulations of QCD with dynamical quarks because of the absence of the baryonic mean field. The results show that in the simulations of the low-energy photon, as well as for the pion vector and scalar forms factors, the vector and scalar form factors, in general, are similar but deviate from each other at $Q^2$ less than one standard deviation. This indicates that for a given observable, the quark loop and baryonic mean field contributions are comparable in magnitude.

For the calculation of the vector form factors of the pion for $Q^2>10^3$ and $|t|>1$ (GeV$^4$), the deviation at small $Q^2$ is a factor 2 larger. Some tumor cells also release products that inhibit the immune response; for example by secreting the cytokine TGF-β, which suppresses the activity of macrophages and lymphocytes.
In general, tumor cells often have mutations in their genome that result in changes in the expression of cell surface antigens and/or the surface levels of MHC-I class I antigens. Tumor cells often evade immune surveillance by reducing expression of several cell surface or secreted proteins that would otherwise activate immune cells.
The ability of a tumor to protect itself from immune attack by downregulating expression of MHC class I antigens limits the potential of antitumor therapies using immunostimulatory genes.
It is useful to be able to induce immune tolerance and immune ignorance in tumor cells by targeting cell surface components of the immune system, such as the CD3, CD14 and CD40 families of proteins. Also, it is useful to be able to inactivate antigen-specific T cells, such as cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), at the tumor site by blocking the antigen-binding sites of MHC class I molecules.
A major problem is the low frequency of T cells in the tumor, especially those CD8.
In contrast to normal T cells, which are relatively rare, tumor-infiltrating CTLs are relatively common. Without legal and reliable way of tracing and knowing who own the property, the tax authorities generally not only do not know who these people are, that is, who are its owners the unregistered property becomes an additional tax evasion tool on the country's tax revenue (IRS 2013d).

Title deeds are the official evidence or paper trail by which an owner of a piece of land can prove the ownership of the land in relation to the legal ownership of land. A title deed is the only legally binding document for establishing, proving, or transferring ownership of property and therefore title deeds are a key and essential mechanism for establishing ownership rights, in most cases, and also when a business entity or other type of economic relationship exists between the people on the land (IRS 2013c). Although it is generally accepted that EU law has primacy, not all EU laws give citizens standing to bring claims: that is, not all EU laws have "direct effect". In Van Gend en Loos v Nederlandse Administratie der Belastingen it was held that the provisions of the Treaties (and EU Regulations) are directly effective, if they are (1) clear and unambiguous (2) unconditional, and (3) did not require EU or national authorities to take further action to implement them. Van Gend en Loos, a postal company, claimed that what is now TFEU article 30 prevented the Dutch Customs Authorities charging tariffs, when it imported urea-formaldehyde plastics from Germany to the Netherlands. When the company requested permission to file an action against the Germans under article 226/3, they were refused. This decision of the Dutch court went against the EU Court of Justice's decision in Linder v Germany.

Van Gend en Loos was contested in the Court of Justice of the EU by Germany and Italy. The Court unanimously found in favour of the Netherlands. In particular the Court declared it to be clear and unambiguous, and, furthermore the claim failed to take the additional step of satisfying that the national government did not act in "an exceptionally serious manner".

The Court was confronted, as always, with a dispute as to how far the Treaty was open to interpretation; in this particular case the dispute was as to whether the law was not merely "inadequate and imperfect", but in fact incapable of serving its purpose of achieving all the EU's objectives.

In addition to finding for the Netherlands, the Court of Justice was also faced with the need to interpret the Treaty to avoid a "significant risk of incompatibility". If its provisions can be seen as being incapable of serving a purpose, the Treaty is at greater risk of becoming unenforceable.

In its decision the Court took into account several factors, among them a review of EU law on the issue, case law from other (former) European courts, and other relevant EU legislation.

Decision problems are one of the central objects of study in computational complexity theory. A decision problem is a special type of computational problem whose answer is either yes or no, or alternately either 1 or 0. A decision problem can be viewed as a formal language, where the members of the language are instances whose output is yes, and the non-members are those instances whose output is no. Each member of the language corresponds to a candidate solution and the language is often viewed as a set of questions whose correct answer corresponds to the solution. The decision problem is to decide what question is asked in the language, and then to determine if the answer is yes or yes (or alternatively (1 or 0) depending on the question) or is no (i.e. (0 or 1)). Decision problems can be viewed as questions like Is there an infinite sequence? and Is there any finite sequence? They are also known as question and answer problems in artificial intelligence and computer science, respectively.
There are two major approaches to finding the best answer, the so-called best-first and the greedy approaches. The best-first approach is widely used to find the exact answer quickly, by always picking the first question by the given language in which to start solving for a solution. The greedy approach is generally used to find an answer, either an approximate one (e.g. a valid solution among the top few) or no solution at all. The greedy approach has the following nice properties [@hochbaum1994optimal]:
There is at least one solution (namely, one question that correctly answers the language, or alternatively, a valid instance to the language, if there is none yet or if the language contains infinitely many valid instances).

This deforming of the lower solid mantle beneath the asthenosphere, which separates the asthenosphere into deep rift zones and volcanically emplaced plateaus, had been predicted by the great early oceanographicist Georg W. F. Herling and his son, the early oceanographer Christian. He had discovered that the plastically deforming asthenosphere and spreading upper mantle are not connected to each other, and instead the asthenosphere is separated from the upper mantle by great spreading ridges.
But how exactly the asthenosphere spreads over and around the surface of the Earth is of great interest because the spreading is an essential part of the life cycle of the planets. A study of the spreading and rheology of continents and oceanic plateaus indicates that the deforming of the asthenosphere is the process responsible for the rifting from tectonic plate to plate. If this process proceeds uniformly from one plate to another, spreading ridges will separate the asthenosphere into oceanic plateaus and continents. In other words, the process was supposed to show the end-point of great continental plates, but it also shows the beginning of subduction, when plates subside with each other and merge. Therefore, this process is probably one of the essential processes allowing plate tectonics to occur, and when it occurs a continent-ocean boundary is formed. On the eve of the second world war, Winston Churchill was reflecting on the events that had led him to make a series of decisions that led to World War II, but his tone of voice was noticeably at odds with his words. His tone was angry, even furious, as he spoke not of a "madman", but a "fiend". His description of those responsible for World War II would one day be proven to be accurate, but as an observer it could be argued that he had gone too far in his anger. Churchill was referring to his actions during the first world war and in the build-up to the war itself, as well as what he had done in the last months of the war. He had no idea how right he would turn out to be in hindsight.

On 11 December 1941, a date which is not etched into the collective memory until modern video cameras, Britain became the second country to enter an enemy-occupied territory in their conflict with Nazi Germany. The date is significant in that in 1918, Germany was forced to sign a treaty whereby it had agreed to abandon all claims to territory not occupied by Germany in the First World War and the Versailles Treaty. In the Second World War, Hitler was determined to make a similar treaty with Britain, thus putting pressure on the British Government to negotiate on what was now, in their eyes, a purely military issue.

For Churchill, this conflict was a direct conflict with Adolf Hitler.

Dendritic cells (DC) are phagocytes in tissues that are in contact with the external environment; therefore, they are located mainly in the skin, nose, lungs, stomach, and intestines. They are named for their resemblance to neuronal dendrites, as both have many spine-like projections, but dendritic cells are in no way connected to the nervous system. Dendritic cells serve as a link between the bodily tissues and the innate and adaptive immune systems, as they present antigens to T cells, one of the key cell types of the adaptive immune system. Dendritic cells present antigens by binding to them with specific surface receptors. B cells recognize antigens as self, so dendritic cells can induce anti-self-specific B cell immunity ([@B18]). Dendritic cells act as antigen-presenting cells for T cells as DC-activated T cells secrete cytokines, chemokines, and other inflammatory mediators such as interferons that prime T cells in vitro ([@B26]).

Dendritic cell subsets in the skin {#S1}
==================================

Dendritic cells are identified from the skin by expression of cell surface antigens ([@B18]). The tentacles of cydippid ctenophores are typically fringed with tentilla ("little tentacles"), although a few genera have simple tentacles without these sidebranches. The tentacles and tentilla are densely covered with microscopic colloblasts that capture prey by sticking to it. Colloblasts are specialized mushroom-shaped cells in the outer layer of the epidermis, and have three main components: a domed head with vesicles (chambers) that contain adhesive; a stalk that anchors the cell in the lower layer of the epidermis or in the mesoglea; and a spiral thread that coils round the stalk and is attached to the head and to the root of the stalk.

Ctenophores are the dominant organisms forming coral reefs, and they are particularly significant in that they provide a significant proportion of the biomass of the reef community. Ctenophores are among the largest known animals, and are well-known as reef dwellers that play an important role in the ecosystem, because their tentacles play a key role in holding and capturing prey.

There is considerable evidence that this attachment organelle also plays a role in the symbioses of other heterokont plant and animal symbionts, especially in the symbiotic associations of Rhizaria, a diverse group of unicellular, heterotrophic, unelongated plants whose colonies are common in symbiotic associations with the animals of the class Excavata (see above). In the Rhizaria, the colloblasts (Fig. 8.1) are responsible for holding mucilage to the root system of the Rhizidia, which in turn are symbiotic partners that live on a filament, a root-like structure that serves a feeding and anchoring function for the Rhizidia. Thus, the mucilage-attachment complex in the symbionts of Rhodophyta and Chlorophyta are probably the result of a common evolutionary history. The colloblasts in Collozia appear to be homologous, however, in that they are closely similar, and in their attachment to the mucilage-producing root system of the symbiotic partners; and they probably originate from a common ancestral state. Thus Rhizaria and Collozia probably have a common evolutionary origin, and are closely related.

The name Rijn, from here on, is used only for smaller streams farther to the north, which together formed the main river Rhine in Roman times. Though they retained the name, these streams no longer carry water from the Rhine, but are used for draining the surrounding land and polders. From Wijk bij Duurstede, the old north branch of the Rhine is called Kromme Rijn ("Bent Rhine") past Utrecht, first Leidse Rijn ("Rhine of Leiden") and then, Oude Rijn ("Old Rhine").

The modern Dutch name for the modern Rijn (Rijn River), Rijnnek, is a combination of two places names - Roode and Wijken - combined by a suffix -nek. It has been given the common name Nieuwe Rijn ("New Rijn"). The river is sometimes confused with the larger Nieuwe Meer ("New Meer") which has the same meaning, though there are often differences in the character of the water. 

The term Nieuwe Rijn originally (but not always anymore) had a religious meaning, as a name in God's name (cf. Nieuw Rijn). In the past, when the Rhine had been dried up and could no longer flow, the inhabitants of the areas adjacent to the Rhine or Rijn found it profitable to use the names of their churches. This is seen in part of the city of Utrecht, for example. The word Nieuwe Rijn has also often had a derogatory meaning, the commonest being the meaning of a word meaning "new" (as in new-fangled).

a newly developed short double - balloon enteroscope with a working channel enlarged to a diameter of 3.2 mm is a novel innovation in stent placement for patients with surgically altered anatomies . herein , we report three patients in whom this new scope contributed to an efficient technique and ideal treatment . in the first case ,  the double guidewire technique was efficient and effective for multiple stent placements . in the second patient, the new scope was the sole means of manipulating the two guidewires in the ileocecal angle. and, in the third patient, the double guidewire method was the only method available for advancing the stents in the distal ileum and thereby establishing the diagnosis of malignant stricture. All of these stent placements were ultimately successfully established and retained without the need for repeated endoscope procedures.

In the past, gastrointestinal tract stenting procedures were always performed via a rigid scope, and the procedures are now often carried out with non-rigid double-diameter endoscopes. Our case series illustrates many difficulties with the use of a single rigid scope for stent placement in the small-bowel and ileocecal angle. In fact, the double-guidewire method developed for enterolithotomy stent placement may not be appropriate for all such procedures, and the use of a non-rigid double-diameter scope with a diameter of 3.2 mm may be more effective for such procedures because it enlarges the working channel, which is more appropriate for the ileocecal intubation or ligation, and eliminates the need for dilatation. In addition, this endoscope can be easily grasped and advanced through the narrow space in the jejunum and ileum to reach the ileocecal intubation point or to insert the endoscope into the ileocecal angle. As a result, the double-guidewire method using a non-rigid scope should be more appropriate for stent placement in the small-bowel and ileocecal angle. In the programming language, a non-re-occurring function problem is a function problem where there are at least two output values out of which exactly one is more complex than a function of two variables. They fled to the Dutch borderlands, the Spanish Netherlands, and France itself, and settled mostly in the southern part of the country. The tradition that became the Hallstatt-Welf tradition is named after a village of the La Tène culture, the seat of the Welf tradition. If the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom, acting on the advice of the Law Officers in Scotland, decides that particular provisions of the Bill or any parts of it would exceed the constitutional powers of the Scottish Parliament to enact legislation, that part of the Bill cannot be passed without that decision and is therefore rejected. Such a decision can only be made after consultation with Scottish lawyers and/or a Law Officer appointed by the UK Government, and is, in theory, binding on all parliaments of the United Kingdom and all other parliaments of the world. Helper T cells express T cell receptors (TCR) that recognize antigen bound to Class II MHC molecules. The MHC:antigen complex is also recognized by the helper cell's CD4 co-receptor, which recruits molecules inside the T cell (e.g., Lck) that are responsible for the T cell's activation. Helper T cells have a weaker association with the MHC:antigen complex than observed for killer T cells, meaning many receptors (around 200–300) on the helper T cell must be bound by an MHC:antigen in order to activate the helper cell, while killer T cells can be activated by engagement of a single MHC:antigen molecule. The activation of helper T cells involves cross-linking TCR signaling molecules.

The MHC can only bind to antigen in one orientation (symmetric loading, positive co-stimulation), whereas antigen has many possible orientations (heterogenous loading, positive co-stimulation). The helper T cell must not only learn how to differentiate between which of many possible antigen-presenting molecules it should approach—the T cell receptor or the major histocompatibility complex—to recognize an antigen, but also which MHC molecule to associate with its cognate antigen for maximal activation.

Although the MHC class II MHC can bind to antigen in one orientation, the positive co-stimulatory signaling pathway uses multiple co-stimulatory molecules (CD80, CD86, CD152, CD200) on the target cell, which then combine with the B7/CD28 receptor on the T cell and result in upregulation of intracellular and/or surface CD28.

Ranging from about 1 millimeter (0.039 in) to 1.5 meters (4.9 ft) in size, ctenophores are the largest non-colonial animals that use cilia ("hairs") as their main method of locomotion. Most species have eight strips, called comb rows, that run the length of their bodies and bear comb-like bands of cilia, called "ctenes," stacked along the comb rows so that when the cilia beat, those of each comb touch the comb below. The name "ctenophora" means "comb-bearing", from the Greek κτείς (stem-form κτεν-) meaning "comb" and the Greek suffix -φορος meaning "carrying". For most of the year each comb is free, but during certain periods of the year, such as in winter, when there are fewer comb rows, ctenophores can be thought of as holding their ctene-bearing comb rows up out of the water. When this is active, the comb rows are free, or unfed. In the spring, when there are new comb rows, or ctenes, the cenosema is shed, returning the ctene-bearing comb rows to their unfed state, and the animal re-occupies its normal feeding position.

History and classification
The first ctenophore was discovered in 1867, by French zoologist Adrien Marie Rondelle in the stomach of a porpoise at the Paris Zoo.  The type specimen was collected on July 12, 1868 by Jules Léveillé de Lardin who transferred it to the museum of Natural History at the Institut Pasteur. Rondelle named the animal Trichiurus, deriving it from the Greek word for a triptych, θρ

Pathogens can rapidly evolve and adapt, and thereby avoid detection and neutralization by the immune system; however, multiple defense mechanisms have also evolved to recognize and neutralize pathogens. Even simple unicellular organisms such as bacteria possess a rudimentary immune system, in the form of enzymes that protect against bacteriophage infections. Other basic immune mechanisms evolved in ancient eukaryotes and remain in their modern descendants, such as plants and invertebrates.
Immunity is generally classically viewed as being provided by the innate immune system, in which the adaptive immune defenses are activated by pathogens through immunization. The innate immune system is important for providing the first line of defense in defending against disease-causing microorganisms, which are generally found in the normal microflora of nearly all species. In humans, for example, as many as 40% of the population are thought to be susceptible to pathogens, based on data obtained from studies of individuals with weak or defective immune systems.
